https://www.wired.com/story/silicon-vall.markdown:
Silicon Valley is trying to make sense of the growing backlash against artificial intelligence, but so far, it’s not going that well. The inconvenient truth is that a significant portion of the world is not optimistic about the technology they’re building. But recent attempts to diagnose the root of the problem by CEOs like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei indicate they don’t understand what’s actually driving society’s disdain for AI.

The rest of popular culture, meanwhile, is finding ways to capitalize on AI hate. Just look at this new commercial for Liquid Death and Garage Beer. The two beverage brands teamed up with former Philadelphia Eagles football player and Taylor Swift brother-in-law Jason Kelce, who invited people to pee in bottles and send them to AI data centers. In an interview with Marketing Dive , Liquid Death’s creative lead said the data center backlash was “literally the one thing that unites all Americans right now.”

More than half of Americans under 30 say they are more concerned than excited about AI, a figure that’s grown 24 percent in the last five years, according to a Pew Research Center survey published earlier this week. More than 70 percent of people polled in all age groups say they believe AI will lead to fewer jobs.

But other recent polling data shows that people have broader anxieties about the technology that go far beyond jobs and the data center boom. Americans also think AI will harm young people’s ability to form meaningful relationships , that tech companies should be required to compensate creators whose works were used to train models, and that AI could harm the critical thinking skills of students.

The tech industry often chalks up the AI backlash to a communication and branding problem, but it’s much deeper than that. Hearing different messages around AI made little difference in people’s opinion s on the technology’s societal impact, according to a recent survey from the Searchlight Institute.

While Silicon Valley is starting to grapple with growing negative public sentiment about AI, investors and executives I talk to have grown increasingly worried that the industry is failing to fully comprehend how big of a problem this could be for adoption of AI products.

Earlier this month, Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word essay painting his optimistic vision of an AI future. The Meta CEO described a world in which everyone has a personalized AI assistant that knows you intimately (presumably from all the personal information Meta’s apps have collected) and can help with your career, hobbies, and perhaps even raising your children. Of course, such a product doesn’t exist yet, but Zuckerberg is basically arguing that giving everyone unfettered access to highly capable AI is the best-case scenario for this technology.

I’m optimistic that AI will continue getting better and more helpful, but I’m skeptical that this will be enough to transform the way people feel about it. For people to even use the theoretical product Zuckerberg envisions, they will need to have a lot of trust in the companies that build it. Current polling suggests that the AI industry has yet to earn that trust.

The Meta CEO also made a not-so-subtle jab at Amodei, saying he was surprised that “discourse from many developing AI is so filled with doom.” On social media and during an appearance on the All-In podcast, tech investor Gavin Baker reiterated Zuckerberg’s points and went even further, writing that “Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban data centers here in America.” White House AI adviser and All-In co-host David Sacks chimed in as well, writing that Anthropic’s “narratives have done more than anything to shape public fear.”

These comments prompted a rare public response from Amodei, who published a lengthy social media post in which he rejected the idea that his messaging was the culprit of the AI backlash.

“I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust,” Amodei wrote. “I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it.”

Amodei’s initial assertions ring closer to the truth, but he loses me later on. He went on to write that “the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world.” One example he cites is the promise that AI will find a cure for cancer, a goal he’s previously said that people should reasonably expect the technology to achieve.

Amodei, and Silicon Valley broadly, may be missing the forest for the trees here. The AI backlash was not caused by scary warnings about the future from tech CEOs, or the fact that OpenAI and Anthropic have not yet cured cancer. It’s about the ways AI is already starting to change society, which many Americans fear is for the worse.

Tech companies have spent enormous effort making physical data centers more digestible to the public, with promises around responsible water usage, clean energy commitments, and investments in local communities. But unfortunately for them, there’s a lot of evidence suggesting that the data center buildout has simply become the physical manifestation of people’s hatred of AI and the ways tech companies engage with communities overall .

I often talk to rank-and-file employees at AI companies who understand these issues and hear about the backlash from their own families and friends across the country. But the leaders at the center of the AI boom still appear to be unprepared to address all the ways in which AI is changing the world. Silicon Valley will need to find a way to confront these issues more directly in the future if it wants people to fully embrace the products it’s building.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter . Read previous newsletters here.

https://www.wired.com/story/spirit-airli.markdown:
Spirit Airlines may have declared bankruptcy this spring, but the budget airline is still worth something—to AI giants, at least. In mid-August, Google won a $10 million bid to purchase some 34 years of the airline’s data, from invoices and flight operations information to Wi-Fi sales, employee records, and crew pairings.

In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models .” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge.

If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems.

The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!”

The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars , as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI , Anthropic , and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI.

But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say.

“There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.”

In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions . Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals , cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them.

The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records.

The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9.

One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment.

The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says.

In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information.

Though the flight attendants’ objections are just a small part of the larger Spirit Airlines bankruptcy proceeding, the outcome could have a major effect on how labor unions and companies think about employee data going forward, says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine, who studies privacy and technology.

“In a world where billions and trillions are being spent on [ large language models ], anything where words are used is subject to its own profit-making purpose,” he says. “If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.”

The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value. “All workers bring an immense amount of knowledge,” Patel says. “Now artificial intelligence has given us the ability to process all different kinds of data.”

More value, meanwhile, is one of the former Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ goals. Separately, the union has also intervened in the bankruptcy to demand roughly $68 million in unpaid vacation, health care, and back pay.

“We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.

https://www.wired.com/story/teachers-dee.markdown:
For Luis DeSantiago, a substitute teacher in Los Banos, California, it started with a few text messages. On March 12, as he was working his other part-time job at a coffee shop, his phone lit up. A fellow barista said there was an AI photo circulating on social media. Her cousin wanted to know if it was DeSantiago.

At first, DeSantiago wasn’t worried—he figured that inappropriate photos violated TikTok’s community guidelines and were usually quickly removed.

“When I finally saw the image, that’s when it felt like a punch to the gut,” DeSantiago tells WIRED. Parts of it resembled a mirror selfie that he remembered taking at a job in college. But instead of his work uniform, he was wearing lingerie. And instead of standing normally, as he had been in the original photo, he was posing suggestively.

The texts kicked off a monthslong saga that crossed two schools and involved students and administrators. And DeSantiago is far from the only educator who’s been victimized this way.

WIRED spoke with three other teachers who allege that their students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI. They say the incidents have been profoundly distressing and disappointing—and in some cases, it’s led them to reassess how they view their work and their relationships with their students.

## “This Could Include Other Students”

After he received the texts, DeSantiago began to piece together who might have been behind the image. One account that shared it used their real name in their TikTok profile—it was a student DeSantiago knew from the local middle school, where he regularly filled in. DeSantiago suspected the involvement of two other students based on people who followed and interacted with that account, and his knowledge of student friend groups. He was scheduled to work at that very middle school the next day.

DeSantiago reported the incident to the assistant principal, who assured him that the school would "take care of it.” Later that evening, he decided to look for the image by searching his name on TikTok. He discovered that a different student had created an account impersonating him—it used his name, slightly mispelled, and had the same photo as their profile picture.

Over the next few weeks, DeSantiago says, he went back and forth with school administrators, the parents of the students, and even the police.

“If these students aren't afraid of generating and posting these images of me, I am concerned of what they may be circulating privately through text messages and group chats,” DeSantiago wrote to the principal. “Keep in mind this could include other students as well.”

One student, who admitted to creating the image, was disciplined with in-school suspension. DeSantiago was later told that the image was also shared on Snapchat. But DeSantiago says the image continued to proliferate, and other students began posting it. He says he also received several crude, sexual comments on his TikTok account.

DeSantiago told administrators he didn’t want to take assignments at the middle school “until this matter is fully addressed.” The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

He took a substitute assignment at the local high school, but the problems followed him. During one class, he received an AirDropped photo of the same AI-generated image before it was quickly revoked. He could tell it was circulating among the class.

The principal told him the school was launching an “immediate investigation” and offered to meet with DeSantiago or make the school counselor available, but DeSantiago says he probably won’t return to the district this year.

He tells WIRED that, at least right now, he doesn’t feel safe doing so.

## “It Makes You Question Everything”

When fake nude images of nonconsenting adults are disseminated, it could constitute cyberstalking and violate the federal Take It Down Act , which makes it a crime to publish nonconsensual “intimate visual depictions of individuals, both authentic and computer-generated,” on the internet.

In most of the accounts shared with WIRED, the teachers didn't directly report the content to the platforms on which it appeared. Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy shared the company's policies on harassment and sexual content , which prohibit sharing AI-generated or manipulated content to humiliate or sexually harass others. She told WIRED that the company has "established processes" for reporting such content, and that it continues to "develop features and tools designed to support the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." TikTok did not provide comment before publication.

Donna Ballman, a retired employment advocacy lawyer, tells WIRED that if a student creates and shares sexual images of a teacher, it constitutes a “clear case” of sexual harassment in the workplace.

Ballman says that under federal antidiscrimination laws, employers have an obligation to create a workplace free of sexual harassment. In a school, this could mean disciplining the student or moving them to a different classroom. She adds, however, that there's “no blueprint” for how schools need to respond to these incidents. Administrators don’t even have to tell a victimized teacher how a student may have been disciplined.

“They just have to make [and] create a safe environment for the victim,” Ballman says.

One middle school teacher in her mid-twenties tells WIRED that she’s seen so much AI-generated content used to harass teachers that she’s bracing for the next wave. (She requested anonymity because she did not have permission from her school district to speak about her experience.)

Last year, she says, students found public photos of a teacher in her sixties, manipulated them to make it appear that she was committing sex acts, and shared them with each other in a Snapchat group chat.

A few months ago, the teacher says, she learned from a student about a TikTok account impersonating her. It looked AI-generated—her face had the characteristic smoothness of AI-generated content, her mouth was moving unnaturally while speaking, and the sound of her voice didn’t match her own. Some of the videos showed her doing things like skydiving or backflips. But others depicted her talking about sexual acts she performed and enjoyed.

She says she told her principal about the account and that they assured her that they would “see what we can do.” Throughout the day, students continued to warn her about the account. She says that some told her that they knew who made the account—one of their classmates. She says the student was known to have behavioral problems.

“I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me genuinely believed that was my account, and that I was saying those things,” she tells WIRED. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, you guys—that is not me.’” She asked them to report it to TikTok, and she says the account was quickly taken down.

Still unnerved by the incident, she mentioned the TikTok account during the next monthly teacher meeting. A colleague said he had seen a seemingly AI-generated fake video of himself getting arrested, which he believed was generated by the same student.

As days and weeks passed, she says, she became the target of escalating, in-person harassment from this same student, who began “cursing me out, calling me names, telling me to fuck off, calling me a bitch.” She raised it at the next faculty meeting, and the assistant principal said that the same student was calling and texting them in the middle of the night and posting apparent AI-generated photos of them to TikTok.

She says the principal removed the student from her class and tried to limit his access to her. But she says that the harassment continued until the student ultimately left the district, and TikTok removed the account.

She says that these behavioral issues aren’t exclusive to this particular student. “It's kind of unsurprising that we are dealing with that, because these kids just have a hard time,” she says. "I'm just worried about this happening again.”

Other teachers say their experiences have fundamentally changed the way they relate to students.

Alice, who asked to be identified by her first name, works for a UK college that trains students aged 16 to 19 in trades like construction. Her job combines administrative responsibilities, like taking attendance, with the role of a college counselor. She says she individually meets with about 150 students throughout the year and takes pride in being able to be a sounding board, give them advice, and serve as a mentor.

This winter, she says, school administrators told her that a student filed a report claiming two videos were circulating among his classmates. One appeared to be real, and it showed her having a conversation with a student. The other one, they said, appeared to be a manipulated version of the first. But instead of talking to the student, it showed her taking her clothes off and dancing around in what was either underwear or a bikini.

Alice tells WIRED that as a qualified youth worker, part of her job often involves talking about things that students may feel “too embarrassed to tell their parents about,” like drugs, parties, or having safe sex. She says she had several of those conversations with the student she suspected had created the video. The student denied it when questioned by administrators and soon dropped out of the school. (The college did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“It makes me reflect as well on those conversations, thinking, did he think that he could overstep a line because we were having these discussions?” she says. “It makes you question everything,” she says.

Afterward, the college gave her permission to step away from the class for a few weeks and took steps to educate students about the danger of creating or distributing deepfakes. But when she returned, she says, the atmosphere had chilled.

“I did have a really good rapport with my students—I do have a good rapport with my students,” she says. And she still loves her work. “But it's definitely made me a bit more cautious, a bit more vigilant when it comes to folks.”

## “It Crosses the Line”

Like DeSantiago, Arizona-based sixth-grade teacher Luke Red says his students circulated an AI-generated photo of him in the comments of his public TikTok account. The image depicted him and another male teacher kissing each other.

Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok—not for content violations but for being under the minimum age of 13—but says TikTok didn’t remove the accounts. He says that the school immediately launched an investigation and quickly identified the student, who admitted to creating and sharing the image. The student received a three-day suspension—the most severe punishment kids their age can receive for a first-time sexual harassment offense, according to the school district handbook. The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Red tells WIRED that reflecting on the experience “has kind of sent me into a spiral.” His concerns, he says, are not necessarily about what happened to him. They’re more focused on the enthusiastic, permissive culture surrounding AI use among his students.

“It just got to the point where students felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images,” Red says. “Obviously when you're making your teachers do sexual things with these images, that's where it crosses the line.”

Ultimately, he feels more sorry for the students than for himself.

“It's just clear [that] so many kids nowadays just don't understand not only how what they're doing can affect others, but just what happens on the internet and how dangerous it can be,” Red says.

https://www.wired.com/story/tech-visiona.markdown:
Tim O’Reilly’s yardstick for measuring the worth of a company, person, or society has long been create more value than you capture. It’s no surprise that O’Reilly— publisher , internet pioneer , VC , conference organizer, and dispenser of tech wisdom —is applying that metric to the way people design and use AI. Specifically, he’s pushing for a future where open-source AI is an elixir for the masses. He worries that, like Microsoft in the 1990s, today’s hyperscalers are trying to lock users into their products. So he is promoting efforts to open-source AI technology—not only making critical technical details such as neural-net weights accessible, but unlocking the whole stack of an AI system, giving control to designers and users.

O’Reilly sees AI as a new creative medium, which he uses extensively—and even has a blog about his chats with it. During our conversation, we discovered that we disagree about AI’s role in producing original content. Guess who took which side.

STEVEN LEVY: You are all in on open-source AI. Make your case.

TIM O'REILLY: First, let's make sure we're talking about the same thing. When most people talk about open-source AI, they're really just talking about open-weight models. It’s much bigger than that. In the ’90s, when everybody else was focused on open-source licenses, I was like, “No, no, it's about the architecture of the system. Does it enable participation?”

Why is that needed?

The big labs are reading the future wrong. They have told themselves a narrative where having the biggest, best model is the key to the future. Big models like Claude are optimizing for particular use cases, but they aren't necessarily the use cases that people want . I want to embed my own special sauce. The most important thing is having a clean separation between the model, the harness , and the application. And right now we're not getting that. They built an architecture of control rather than an architecture of freedom and participation, so they have the ability to track you.

Isn’t it against the interests of big companies to give up control?

Oh, it's totally against their interests. But that doesn't mean that they're making the right strategic decision. For a long time, the latest and greatest models were really better for everything. Now they’re better for some things and worse for others. People are talking a lot about how Fable and Sol are worse writers than the lower-level models. [Note: Anthropic and OpenAI would disagree.] The breakthroughs that we're getting in so-called frontier AI are actually pushing us further away from what ordinary people are going to need. We could win frontier AI here in the US, and China will kick our ass because they have lower-level models diffused widely through society. The goal is to give people the ability to innovate freely, to paint outside the lines.

People worry that open-source software can be a security risk, since bad actors will be able to jump the frontier model’s guardrails.

All of the cybersecurity incidents we’ve seen are from the frontier models . So risks like cybersecurity and the ability to develop pathogens are actually an argument for slowing down the frontier models more than an argument for restricting open-weight models.

So you feel that with open source the AI powers will no longer be dominant?

I don't predict the future. but I will say the world is proceeding the way that I hoped it would. What if the big frontier models end up like mainframes or supercomputers—aimed at really hard problems, which are not actually the thing that gets diffused throughout society? People are building things like Pi , an open-source [agentic] harness. One of the things we're working on at my nonprofit, the AI Disclosures Project , is the idea of an open-memory consortium. Mark Zuckerberg’s thesis is, he’s going to lock you in because Meta will give you the AI that knows you best. The open-source vision needs to say no to this. Open source can give you the ability to switch models, switch providers, and maintain all the context that it needs.

You recently wrote a piece in the Economist about how Elon Musk—as well as other tech leaders—have so much power in their companies that they are anti-capitalist, in the sense that their desires, rather than the marketplace, determine strategy.

In general, Silicon Valley has become anti-capitalist. They use the language of markets. But around 2010, the whole model came into play with Uber and Lyft. Funded by VCs, they literally spent billions of dollars to subsidize rides. The venture capitalists picked the winner rather than the market. That became the template. All the capital piles on and chokes out other possible paths.

In AI, all the money is funneling into a few companies, but none seem to have a lock.

Because it's a failed model. The real action is open source. Just like in the early 1990s, when everybody thought it was all a battle for who ruled the PC, and then the web came out of left field while nobody was paying attention. I think that the real AI future will be a ferment of innovation that's not being funded by venture capital—in the same way that the web wasn't funded by VCs.

One of those disruptions might be your own company, built on books and writing.

The book business has been in decline for 25 years. At our peak, our book business was maybe $70 million, and it's now $30 million. As books generated less revenue, we had to find a way to compensate people for sharing their knowledge, because that's our fundamental business. So now AI comes along and hoovers everything up. Can we build a set of tools that help people with that? Being able to invoke the knowledge of experts is a superpower, and we have to figure out what that looks like now.

When I edit this interview I will boil down our long conversation to a shorter one, but I won’t use AI to do it. And of course, the writing in the introduction will be all mine. It’s actually our policy.

I think that's a legacy thing that's going to go. My ability to have a thought partner in AI when I'm writing is very powerful.

AI does your writing for you?

No, no. I use it for brainstorming, and sort of just functional writing. When I interview somebody for an hour, I go to AI and say, “Turn it into something I can use.” I don't have the time to write up all those interviews.

Aren’t you worried that AI will eventually supplant human writing?

AI is literally a medium, in the same way that written words are a medium, or paint or music is a medium. When I talk to an AI or design art with it, I get something different out of it than you do, in the same way that Michelangelo and Van Gogh got completely different things out of paint. The idea that you can't write with AI will seem as curious as the idea that you can't make a good portrait or landscape with a camera. There will be people who are masters at expressing their ideas by summoning words from LLMs. People used to ride horses. Now, few do. We're in the early days.

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter . Read previous newsletters here.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-ai-slop-.markdown:
I was recently digging through my Instagram settings, trying to disable Meta’s now-defunct feature that allowed anyone to create AI deepfakes of me without consent. Anger bubbled up inside as I tapped through the Kafkaesque opt-out process .

Rather than throwing my phone across the room, I blurted to my partner that we should leave San Francisco behind and be off-grid sheep farmers. Something analog . In that moment, anything sounded better than this ongoing, generative-AI-induced hell .

Many Americans are having similar reactions to the growing prevalence of generative AI in daily life . “The AI revolution has happened, and everybody hates it,” says Meredith Broussard , a data journalism professor at New York University and author of Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World . In a recent Gallup poll , Americans’ increased familiarity with generative AI coincides with negative attitudes about the technology. This is especially true for young people between 18 and 29, where almost half see generative AI as doing more harm than good.

While this AI backlash has been brewing for the last few years, more companies appear to be directly addressing these concerns. LinkedIn added a “ seems like AI slop ” button for reporting AI-generated content on the platform, despite still hosting plenty of generative AI tools. Snapchat announced that fully AI-generated videos would no longer be eligible for its discovery feed. Substack recently added an AI detection tool to police writers.

The backlash’s “why” is simple at its core. Many Americans feel like they never consented to any of this. I had no idea that my online interactions would one day be scraped en masse for AI model training. I didn’t ask for Instagram to enable deepfakes on my account. I didn’t want Google to push AI-generated answers at the top of search results. I woke up one day, and generative AI features were stuffed into every corner of all the software I rely on without my consent.

Whether it's AI models scraping your data or noisy data centers popping up in your backyard, the AI revolution seems to be an event happening to us without making us feel like active participants.

“Consent is really important,” Broussard tells WIRED. “We can connect that to the way that women, queer people, people of color, and minorities get exploited and abused online. Tech companies have never really been sensitive to issues of consent.”

Public backlash appears to be working, at times, in getting unwanted AI features shut down. “They just roll them out and see what sticks, because nobody really knows what this is for,” says Nick Seaver , an associate professor of anthropology at Tufts University focusing on technology and society. Google recently rolled back the ability for people to use generative AI to tweak satellite images on Google Earth almost immediately after launching it, following reporting from 404 Media . Additionally, Meta turned off the aforementioned deepfaking tool for Instagram users after three days of public outcry and viral videos with millions of views criticizing the feature.

There’s also a growing rejection of generative AI in marketing materials. Many people online reacted negatively to major brands, like McDonald’s and Coca-Cola , incorporating generative AI visuals into their ad spots. Even local shops see backlash for promoting events using AI-generated posters .

Beyond online outcry, more people are starting to protest against the building of data centers that power these AI tools. “There's a lot of pushback coalescing around data centers," says Emily Bender , coauthor of The AI Con . "Data centers are important because they are focal points of environmental and economic damage.” Americans across the political spectrum have recently united in these data center protests .

While tech workers in San Francisco, especially software developers, have latched on to generative AI tools as central to their everyday work , many of these uses are obligatory. “Top-down mandates to use large language models are crazy,” one Block employee told me during the layoffs earlier this year at Jack Dorsey’s fintech company. “If the tool were good, we’d all just use it.” I don’t want to be forced to use specific tools at work, especially one that’s morally questionable and shown to be wrought with errors .

It’s easy to feel helpless when pushing back against the whims of giant, well-funded tech companies, but the recent rollbacks of some AI features stand as a reminder about the power of collective action. “I would definitely encourage people to organize using traditional methods as well as digital methods,” says Broussard. “Remind people that public pressure works.”

https://www.wired.com/story/the-big-inte.markdown:
If you want a clear understanding of how AI is affecting Hollywood … good luck.

Some of the industry loathes the technology , with screenwriters, directors, and actors alike vowing never to use AI in their work—or collaborate with those who do. Others are much more open to the potential for AI to act as everything from creative partner to cost-cutting engine. And a rare few, Ben Affleck included, are already making millions by capitalizing on AI’s nascent potential to (they argue) streamline and improve the filmmaking process.

At WIRED, we’re constantly doing our best to document AI’s transformational effects on the entertainment business, for better and for worse. (If you haven’t read Ruth Fowler’s recent essay for us, on going from a screenwriter to an underemployed LLM trainer, I highly recommend it.) But in an effort to get the most nuanced possible view, I wanted to talk to someone who knows the industry and its players inside and out.

Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck, has covered Hollywood for decades. He writes a scoopy newsletter ( What I’m Hearing … ) and hosts a scoopy podcast ( The Town ) that frequently focus on AI and Big Tech as both become increasingly dominant forces across entertainment. Belloni also happens to be a former lawyer, making him the ideal person to ask about the ongoing, and highly consequential, debates over AI and copyright, IP, and celebrity likeness.

Belloni was generous enough to give me an hour of his time, and we managed to cover all the bases—from whether Hollywood types side-eyed Ben Affleck after he sold an AI startup to Netflix for $587 million, to just how much control Big Tech companies now wield over the entertainment industry. You can read our conversation above or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Matt, I have to start with the obvious, which is artificial intelligence . You've been on top of AI in Hollywood for a very long time, and you've said multiple times that, quote, “everyone is doing it,” meaning everyone [in the industry] is using AI. What exactly do you mean by that?

MATTHEW BELLONI: Well, there's two types of AI, as you know. There's generative AI, which is content creation and things like that, and then there's what I refer to as the corporate AI, like streamlining processes and better search results. Obviously, on the second one, everyone is using it.

I'm not going to name a name, but I heard a very interesting story about a very prominent showrunner who went into the writer's room and basically castigated her writing team for not using ChatGPT to help with the process.

To help with the creative process? Or the admin and bookkeeping?

The creative process. Here's a scenario, suggest some jokes. Here's this, this, this. It doesn't mean they use them. You could do the same thing with Google. It's just better, and people are using it. I know, I've talked to screenwriters who use it to suggest scenarios or to give a description of the inside of a building where they want a scenario to play out, or things that to me seem like part of the process.

You may not know this, but the Writers Guild is actually OK with that. As long as there is a credited writer on every script and that this process doesn't impact jobs, they're OK with the use of this technology.

That's one side. Then the other side is generative and how this is making content. There it's a little murkier, because there are a lot of studios that are purporting to create AI-generated movies, shorts, TV pilots. I've seen a lot of them. They're not great. They're better in animation, and I think this is where we're going to see the disruption first, but you can always kinda tell, and that's the problem when you're trying to relate to people. I can't wait to see what Elon's historically accurate version of The Odyssey looks like.

I mean, it's obviously going to be spectacular. I'm sure he's hard at work on it. He's probably been staying up all night, all week.

First of all, historically accurate is hilarious for a work of fiction. But it just means it's going to be all white people. And the funny thing is, if he tries to use or to scrape the actual version of [Christopher Nolan’s] The Odyssey —I don't know if you saw the headlines, a full version of The Odyssey leaked on X last weekend, and before Universal could send a takedown, it was viewed like a million times …

I actually had not seen that.

So who knows whether Grok got its hands on the actual Odyssey to train for Elon’s fake Odyssey , but whatever.

On the generative AI front, I think where we’re seeing the biggest innovation/disruption is in the animation world, where visually scenes can be completed and storyboards done without the use of artists. You can extrapolate things. Doesn't mean it's the finished product, but even Netflix , on their earnings call this past month, said that 300 shows use generative AI.

I saw that. And they're talking about that relatively loudly and freely. I'm wondering where the stigma is right now. Are there members of Hollywood—actors, directors, screenwriters—who are calling out AI publicly while using it privately? How much of this is still happening behind closed doors in secretive circumstances?

Well, obviously I don't know what everybody does behind closed doors, but I know what people I talk to say to me. I do know that there is still a taint on using it.

A perfect example is Amazon. They did a whole media day where they brought in press and they have this whole AI generative studio that is being run by Albert Chang, one of their executives, and they announced a bunch of shows, including some animation shows, and there were real creators on these shows.

Almost immediately, the backlash that one of the creators got online was so crazy—I don't say crazy meaning bad, I mean crazy like loud—that he stepped down. That's a tangible impact of AI shaming, so to speak, and that is real.

You know, maybe that'll change. Netflix got a lot of leeway on this, because what did they do? They bought Ben Affleck's AI company. They paid almost 600 …

$587 million. And I barely knew he had an AI company until he sold it.

I asked the question, “Was this a $600 million press release?” Because Netflix wants to get into AI. They know that Ben is someone who has a ton of credibility and cachet as a movie star, an Oscar winner, a filmmaker, and having him attached to this company buys them a lot of leeway and allows them to do things that maybe others would bristle at, but it's Ben’s company. He's vouching for it.

And if you look at what that product actually does, it takes the footage that you have shot, and it makes it available for generative AI, essentially.

So it prevents you from having to do a costly reshoot if all you need is some coverage of something. It allows you to extend the periphery of a scene or get a circle shot when you didn't get it in camera. It’s much more of a tool for filmmakers—or at least this is how they've presented it—than something that is replacing [them], because the big fear in Hollywood is that this technology will replace [people].

What was the talk of the town, so to speak, when Ben made that deal? Did people scratch their heads? Did they look at him differently than they had the day before?

I honestly don't think so. There are a number of filmmakers that are doing this, and doing it the so-called right way. Darren Aronofsky is one of them—and Ben, I think because of his credibility and because he's able to articulate very clearly what he's actually doing and what he's not doing.

Because of that, I think that it went over OK. I think the biggest reaction I heard was like, "Holy cow, $600 million?"

That's a lot of money.

He's gonna make more money on that than he's made on any of his movies put together.

Well, he's had some, I don't know, expensive divorces.

I know. The question is, did he launch it when he was married to JLo? I imagine their prenups probably contemplate their separate property.

I think they had a very expensive house they were trying to offload at one point. I'm a big entertainment gossip reader.

There have been a bunch of deals between tech firms and Hollywood. There was the $75 million investment from Google DeepMind into A24, which pissed a lot of fans off . You had Lionsgate taking a stake in Runway , which is a big name in AI-generated video.

Why is this happening? Is it that the technology is ready? Is it that Hollywood is more receptive to this idea that, potentially, the technology can really have an impact on the industry?

I think there's a couple things. First of all, the technology is better, and it is applicable, and there's this fear in the C-suites of the entertainment companies of being left behind. If you talk to people at the studios, one of the biggest problems they face is the cost of movies. The cost of movies keeps going up, whereas the box office is not necessarily covering that.

If you look at the animation space, Pixar is a perfect example. Pixar originals, they can't make them for less than $200 million. I mean, they can, but it's very difficult to make them. They're made in California with a California workforce. They have their own special process that is very labor-intensive, and they haven't used AI to the extent that they maybe could.

If we are looking at a new landscape where movies just aren't going to gross as much as they did, you have to look at bringing the cost down.

And the guilds aren't bringing the cost of labor down. The unions are not willing to do that. So where does it come from? It comes from non-unionized labor that is, for the most part, the below-the-line people and the technology.

That makes me think of Christopher Nolan and The Odyssey . It had a huge cast, it was made all over the world. It's making crazy money. And Chris Nolan, who I believe still professes to not having a phone, not surprisingly has also been critical of AI while also being open to its uses, right?

He's kind of a fence-sitter. But he has also pointed out that younger generations have rejected a lot of quote-unquote slop, right? They're looking for authenticity. That said, are the Chris Nolans of the world going to continue to be even more the exception to the rule?

He is a one of one at this point, where he came into this situation with all the credibility and clout in the world, having won the Oscar for Oppenheimer and having made a billion dollars off that movie. The Odyssey , if it is made at all by another filmmaker, it's made at a much lower cost, not $250, almost $300 million. You don't get to have all those stars in it. You just don't get to do it.

But what I would argue to the studios is that is exactly why it broke through, is that it smells different. If you look at the trailer, if you look at everything around it, it smells authored, and the audience can tell when something is authored.

In a world where you can create all the visual effects you want, there's something about seeing The Odyssey and knowing, because they are very good at marketing this, that this is the vision of one guy who you trust and who is gonna show you something real. And I say real in the sense that movies are increasingly going to be split into movies that are filmed with real people and real scenarios and then those that are just either generative AI in practice or generative AI from the get-go.

There's going to be a split between things that we find authentic and those that we just kind of passively enjoy.

Just sort of consume, for lack of a better term.

That's where social media is going, and the more social video goes that direction, I think the bigger the market opening is for these kinds of big, special, real movies.

But you have a one of one legendary filmmaker like Chris Nolan over here with The Odyssey . Then you have someone like Kane Parsons, who made Backrooms , which made a ton of money for A24. I thi

https://www.wired.com/story/the-friend-2.markdown:
Friend CEO Avi Schiffmann welcomes me into his palace—what he calls his large apartment in San Francisco.

He sits on the couch in his living room, clad in an orange shirt emblazoned with a cartoon version of the motorcycle driven by Italian racer Valentino Rossi. He props his feet up on the side table and leans back, a round, softly glowing circular Friend pendant dangling from a yellow cord around his neck.

This is the second iteration of the Friend necklace , the controversial AI companion device that just about everyone ( me included ) seems to hate. The company announced the device on Thursday through its new X handle .

The first version of Friend was an always-listening AI wearable that responded via text message. The big update here is a speaker on the back that lets the device voice its responses aloud. That has changed the shape of the pendant, as the underside with the speaker is bulkier than before. Its AI chops have also been upgraded, now running OpenAI’s latest models .

Like the first go, Friend aims to be a digital companion users can talk to and hold long conversations with. Unlike the original, each new pendant comes with a random voice and personality already established. The user cannot change the voice or name, so you’re locked in with that Friend. (Your mileage may vary on how friendly the thing actually is to you.)

The new pendant costs $249, a marked increase over the original’s $129 price. You can buy one now on Friend.com , a domain Schiffmann paid $1.8 million for. There is also an optional $10 monthly subscription that lets the AI remember the conversations you’ve had for longer than 30 days. The colorful cord around Schiffmann’s neck is part of an accessories collection he says will be coming later this year.

Schiffmann first garnered headlines in 2020 as a 17-year-old who built a website to track Covid-19 cases during the pandemic. Now 24, he’s far more well known—and outright notorious—for leading a company that makes a device many have called dystopian or like something out of a Black Mirror episode.

“I’ve grown up a lot,” Schiffmann tells me just about every time I see him.

Behind Schiffmann’s couch is a gigantic framed photograph of a Paris subway station with ads for the Friend pendant splayed across the walls. The ads, placed by Schiffmann’s company across New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago in 2025—and Paris in early 2026—sparked vigorous pushback and controversy over AI usage. People graffitied them in protest and griped that they devalued humanity , generating a litany of poignant headlines about the ads. The marketing got much more attention than the actual product ever did. (The art frame he’s got the photo in at home cost $500, Schiffmann tells me later. Update: Schiffmann clarified that it was actually $5,000.)

“Something like Friend is very dystopian in people’s minds and very futuristic,” Schiffmann says. “But we’re presenting it in the most analog way possible.”

That analog component is important to Schiffmann. He says he doesn’t have an internet connection in his home. He listens to music on a record player . He’s shooting a documentary about himself on Kodak Ektachrome . (The film started as a documentary-style version of The Social Network , he says, “but now it’s turning much more into like a Boyhood -style thing.” ) He argues that the controversial ad campaign was also analog, using print media to encourage human interaction.

After the ad campaign peaked, Schiffmann released a series of four user videos highlighting Friend customers. The videos are profoundly weird, often borderline bleak looks at people who suffer from depression or sheer loneliness. He says the move was deliberate to show the real people using his devices.

“That’s life, isn’t it?” Schiffmann says. “I'm so much more intrigued to see how it’s affecting the people in those random Appalachian towns or whatever than it is [creating] slight productivity gains for finance people in New York. I don’t really give a fuck.”

Schiffmann says all of the consternation around Friend—and the resulting media sensations—has been deliberate. He seems to like making people mad, or at least feel something, leading some to ask whether this is all just an elaborate Warhol-esque art display . I ask Schiffmann if this has all just been an elaborate bit, more than an actual product endeavor.

“Reality is so over; everything is ironic now,” Schiffmann says. “Nothing is sacred anymore, and so Friend is both real but also, like, ridiculous. Friend, he acknowledges while wandering around a house where nearly all the art on the walls consists of large paintings he has made himself, is an inherently egomaniacal ambition.

“The whole thing is supposed to be me, in a way, and how I feel,” Schiffmann says. “And it’s encapsulated into a product.”

Still, Friend is very much a product Schiffmann is trying to sell. He says he sold his first run of 5,000 pendants. Now he wants to grow, and aims to sell 50,000 of the second version. (You probably won’t be able to buy one in the European Union, as Schiffmann says he will likely pull the product from the EU because meeting the data privacy rules set by the General Data Protection Regulation makes it too expensive to sell there.)

To hit that goal, Schiffmann’s going to have to convince lots more people to bring this often snarky, funhouse-mirror-style reflection of his character into their lives. He says he understands that people have the impression that Friend users are odd, but he hopes that will change and the product will become more appealing to “normal people.”

In the meantime, his media campaign for the product again focuses on people using the device by themselves or occasionally with another person—asking it whether they’ll ever get married or if their creative works are any good. The videos are vivid, with retro-looking color grading, but there’s always some quiet desperation that the Friend pendant seems to promise more than it can solve.

Schiffmann has a sort of obsession with filmmaking, though he does say that the industry is “played out.” Still, he is involved in all the shoots for his company’s videos. This seems to be his real passion, and the controversy-stirring uncanny AI pals might just be a means to that end.

“How do you make lonely weirdos look cool?” Schiffmann says. “I think it's kind of interesting.”

Correction on July 30 at 12:02 pm ET: Schiffmann says the art frame for his Friend poster is actually $5,000, not $500. We've clarified this in the story.

https://www.wired.com/story/the-most-dan.markdown:
Agentic AI has permanently changed cybersecurity by making it quicker and easier to discover vulnerabilities in software and fix them—or develop so-called exploits to weaponize them. But longtime web security researcher James Kettle wanted to look beyond the bug-hunting apocalypse to explore a question that has taken on even more urgency as major AI organizations disclose real-world examples of rogue AI hacking: Can agentic AI develop novel, abstract hacking methods, from concept through to practical attacks?

At the Black Hat security conference in Las Vegas on Wednesday, Kettle presented his findings, which illustrate both AI’s rapidly advancing cybersecurity capabilities and its limitations. For now, the answer to Kettle’s question is nuanced. He concluded that AI is perhaps minimally capable but extremely limited in its ability to devise new attack paths in a fully autonomous way. Importantly, though, when paired with human guidance and insight in key moments, Kettle found that AI is an extremely powerful partner in conceptualizing and uncovering new strategies for hacking.

After spending years researching web security vulnerabilities , Kettle says he has uncovered an entirely new area of potential vulnerability—dubbed Shared-Parser Confusion—as the result of an AI revelation about web servers using shared code to process both requests and responses.

“This is an absolutely massive deal, because if you think about it, requests to a website are completely untrusted, they could be anything, but responses are trusted,” Kettle told WIRED ahead of his conference talk. “So this is a major attack surface and potentially spills into a lot of different attack types.”

The finding came out of months of experiments that began in September 2025 using Anthropic ’s and OpenAI’s latest models at the time. Kettle wanted to explore AI’s ability to do theoretical security research but quickly realized that one obstacle was that the systems were attempting to pass existing research off as original by returning findings about extremely esoteric topics that were difficult to vet. With this in mind, he decided to scope his tests more narrowly so the AI systems were working within his own area of web security expertise. This way he had total command of the material and knew that AI couldn’t trick him. Additionally, Kettle realized that by synthesizing his own research methodology and training models on it, he could probe deeper into what the systems were capable of extrapolating on their own.

“I’m interested in pushing AI to the absolute limit to see where it fails and where you need a human,” Kettle says. “There are still very few people talking about where the limits are, especially in the security space, because there aren’t incentives to talk about that angle. Everyone wants to be seen as AI native, not talk about where their system falls apart completely.”

As Kettle honed his experiments—providing models with more methodological data and more refined parameters—and as time passed and more powerful models debuted, he says the systems had more and more findings at a rate far surpassing his own, creating what he describes as a productive research feedback loop.

“It was really interesting going through the process. It would have notable findings maybe every two days without me even logging into the system, to the point that it was making me anxious,” Kettle says, “like I almost don’t want to know. It was so many research leads that you have FOMO about not exploring all of them, so it forces you to automate more analysis.”

In addition to finding more proven examples of certain vulnerabilities in a few months than he could likely find in a few years, Kettle also hoped that the AI system could find an entire novel class of those types of bugs. And in a way it did succeed, he says, but the finding related to an extremely rare type of bug and was not actually exploitable in the one vulnerable target available. “It wasn’t able to prove this itself, but it analyzed some real, proven findings and came up with the hypothesis, and I evaluated it and confirmed it,” Kettle says. “That’s probably going to be the discovery that has the biggest long-term impact. It couldn’t do that on its own, but I would never have found that on my own for sure. Even if you gave me the single line from the [documentation], I wouldn’t have seen it. When Tim Millard received an email about interviewing for a media relations job in January, six months into his job hunt, he assumed he’d speak to a human. When he was instead instructed to record himself answering a series of questions on camera, he felt a familiar pang of resignation—one that had followed him throughout the job hunt .

“I figured, I have to do this if I want to be considered for the job,” Millard tells WIRED. So, that evening, the Atlanta-based communications and marketing expert tidied his living room and set up his laptop. The email had left the timing for the interview open-ended, and he figured he might as well get it done as soon as possible. “What else was I going to do at 9:30 at night?”

The questions were pretty standard for the role. How would Millard pitch a story to the media? How would he cultivate relationships with local journalists? But the setup was bizarre. He sat in front of his laptop, watching as a question popped up on the screen. He had roughly half a minute to think about his response.

“Once the 30 seconds was up, ‘ding!’ Now you have two minutes to record your answer,” Millard said. “It felt so out of this world.”

Millard received an automated rejection email in March. But the experience unknowingly wedged him into a trend currently reshaping the modern job search . As automated video interviews and AI become a bigger part of the recruitment process , so do late-night interviews.

Arsham Ghahramani said that he noticed the late-night interview trend almost immediately after he cofounded and launched Ribbon, a company that makes voice-AI recruitment software. Twenty-four percent of Ribbon’s AI interviews take place between 10 pm and 2 am local time, according to data from the more than 500 companies that use the service. For his manufacturing clients, that figure jumps to 35 percent.

“This is a genuinely new option for people,” Ghahramani says. Many parents can’t sacrifice 30 minutes until the clock strikes 10 pm. Same for employees paid hourly, or those who are tied up working their current jobs on a noisy factory floor or kitchen. “Some people are very constrained in their options of when they can interview and how they can interview.”

Ribbon isn’t the only platform charting the rise in late-night interviews. Hiring platform Greenhouse says that roughly 15 to 20 percent of candidates interviewed by its voice agent now schedule an interview at night.

Ophir Samson, who became head of Greenhouse’s voice AI division when the company acquired his startup in May, tells WIRED that he doesn’t think artificial intelligence should replace human interviews. Which is good, because applicants are currently extremely skeptical of AI interviews.

While a Greenhouse survey in May found that nearly two-thirds of job applicants have been interviewed by an AI agent, up 13 points over six months, most people aren’t particularly excited about this development. Thirty-eight percent of American candidates told Greenhouse that they had withdrawn from a hiring process rather than be interviewed by an AI. Another 12 percent said they’d drop out if an AI interview was required.

One of the major stressors for applicants is the lack of transparency on how the footage will be used. Can AI reject them outright because they fail to say a certain buzzword?

While different employers and services vary, the typical AI or automated video interview is evaluated using a rubric that varies from job to job. A welder might be asked about certain technical skills or certifications in a Ribbon interview, Ghahramani says, while a sales role might include an “enthusiasm” score. AI analyzes footage of the interview to evaluate how well the candidate fits the rubric, and assigns them a score. The score is passed along to the recruiter, along with footage of the interview—though, realistically, many of the interviews go unwatched by humans.

Samson describes Greenhouse’s approach to the AI interview as a sort of résumé add-on, a tool that can identify high-scoring candidates who would have otherwise been lost in the deluge of applications. He doesn’t see the AI interview as a choice between human and robot, but a choice between being ghosted and improving the chance of actually speaking to a human interviewer in the next round.

“It’s a shitty time to be a candidate,” Samson says. “Your résumé goes into a black hole. You’re competing with thousands of candidates that are all using AI to write their résumés. So, good candidates can’t stand out.”

That assessment seems to be in line with Millard’s experience. A year after losing his job, he’s still searching. The process has been so emotionally devastating that it inspired Millard to write a one-man show, After Careful Consideration , which debuted at the Atlanta Fringe Festival in May.

When Millard signed on for his late-night interview in January, he wasn’t marveling at the convenience. He just wanted to get “this godawful thing done.”

“In today's job market,” Millard says, “it feels like if you are going to scream, you're going to scream into the void. And nobody is going to hear you.”

Travel just two hours west of Beijing by train, and you’ll find yourself surrounded by the rolling grasslands and ancient cinder cones of Inner Mongolia. This vast, arid land has long been China’s capital of sheep farming and coal mining , but over the last few years, it has become the hottest place in the country to build an AI data center .

In Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia home to about 1.5 million people, nearly 100 data centers have been opened or begun construction since 2016. Chinese companies have pledged to build projects with a combined estimated capacity of 12.5 gigawatts in the city, and over 70 percent of the total commitments have been announced in just the last year, making it one of the fastest growing compute clusters in Asia, according to a research note published by Goldman Sachs last week. For comparison, OpenAI’s $500 billion Stargate Project is set to reach only 10 gigawatts of total capacity when it’s complete.

Chinese companies are flocking to Ulanqab for a number of reasons. The city sits at high elevation on the Inner Mongolian Plateau and has long, cold winters, which means data centers there don’t need to use as much energy to stay cool. It’s also relatively close to Beijing, so data can be transmitted to China’s populous regions with minimum latency. But the most enticing factor has to do with costs. Electricity is cheaper in Inner Mongolia than almost anywhere else in China, driven by both the strong growth of wind and solar energy and an abundant supply of coal.

What’s also interesting is who is building these data centers. For the first time, Chinese AI companies are making big investments in their own infrastructure, rather than renting compute from cloud companies. DeepSeek is reportedly building a massive AI data center in Ulanqab, as are ByteDance, Alibaba, and Xiaohongshu. For years, Chinese AI companies have spent far less on building physical infrastructure than their American peers, despite developing a number of popular AI models with impressive capabilities. The Ulanqab data center boom signals that now they are finally starting to catch up.

There’s just one problem: finding enough water. Ulanqab is about as dry as Denver, getting only roughly 14 inches of rain each year. The local government is already struggling to provide enough water to meet resident demand—before many of the planned data center projects are even up and running. Last month, the local water company in Ulanqab was forced to turn off several waterworks for seven hours each night to mitigate peak demand. The data centers being built in the city will need less water in the winter—weather data from the local government of Ulanqab shows they only require additional water for cooling during two months out of the year—but all of the new infrastructure could still pose a significant environmental challenge for the region.

## The Boonies

Inner Mongolia has been a data center hot spot for at least a decade, long before the current AI boom. Huawei built its first one in Ulanqab in 2016, and Apple followed suit three years later. In 2021, the area was designated as one of the main hubs of a country-wide government project dubbed “ Eastern Data, Western Compute ,” which aims to build data centers in the Western hinterlands of China.

There was one major drawback, though. Because they are located far from China’s populous eastern coast, these data centers initially faced high latency rates when transferring data to the majority of users. As a result, they were initially largely relegated to backup storage—until AI gave them a new purpose. “With the rise of AI in 2022, there was the realization that actually, those remote data centers could be well-utilized for model training,” says Andrew Stokols, a professor at Singapore Management University who studies China’s compute infrastructure. A training run for an AI model can take months and doesn’t require much real-time tinkering, so latency is less of an issue.

Relatively speaking, Ulanqab is also not really that far away. Inner Mongolia is much closer to Beijing and other major metropolitan areas in China than any Western data center hub is. And it’s now connected by two dedicated fiber optics cables built in 2017 and 2019 that reduced average latency speeds to less than five milliseconds, fast enough to support real-time data exchanges like AI inference.

Compared to other data center hubs in China, Ulanqab’s growth seems to have been driven more by commercial demand than government-led investment, Stokols says. As Chinese AI startups like DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Zhiput AI have begun attracting more paying users at home, they have found a viable business case for inference data centers close enough to serve them without excessive latency.

## Powered by Renewables

The Chinese government is excited about building data centers in Inner Mongolia for another reason: It could help absorb the country’s excess capacity of renewable energy. Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, a Singapore-based research center, says there’s a positive correlation between regions in China with the most unused renewable energy and those that have built the most data centers.

In the eyes of the government, this is a win-win strategy. China can catch up to pace of data center construction in the US, while simultaneously increasing demand for renewable energy. So it should come as no surprise that Envision, one of the largest Chinese manufacturers of wind turbines, announced this month that it will build a 2 gigawatt AI data center in Ulanqab connected directly to the company’s own clean power supply.

But experts caution that looking at AI data centers and renewable energy in China as a match made in heaven is too simple of a story. Stokols found in his research that about 37 percent of electricity in Ulanqab still comes from coal. And since data centers need to run around the clock, operators have traditionally favored fossil fuels for their reliability.

“Inner Mongolia has long been the West Virginia of China. It’s a coal country,” says Ma. The region is now racing to replace coal with wind and solar, but it remains unclear how fast that transition will happen or how far it will go. For now, the data centers popping up in China’s remote highlands will have to keep relying on coal to some extent. But “in three years, maybe it will be completely powered by renewables,” Ma says.
